An altimeter is an instrument that measures altitude — meaning, how high something is above a reference point, usually sea level (the average surface level of the ocean).

In plain words: an altimeter tells you how high up you are.
Why altitude needs to be measured

You might wonder — can't you just look down and judge how high you are? In everyday life, maybe. But in many situations, judging height by eye is impossible or dangerously unreliable:

  • A pilot inside a cloud can't see the ground at all.
  • A mountaineer in fog has no visual landmarks.
  • A skydiver in freefall needs to know exactly when to open their parachute.

This is where an altimeter becomes essential. It gives a precise, objective number for how high you are, regardless of visibility or conditions.

The most common type of altimeter — called a barometric altimeter — works by measuring air pressure.

Here's the key idea: the higher you go, the thinner the air becomes, and therefore the lower the air pressure. This relationship between height and pressure is remarkably consistent and predictable. So an altimeter uses a simple logic:

"The air pressure around me right now corresponds to a certain known altitude. Therefore, I am at that altitude."

It continuously converts the surrounding air pressure into an altitude reading — typically shown in feet or meters.

Another common type is the radar altimeter (also called a radio altimeter), used in aircraft. This one works differently: it sends a radio wave straight down toward the ground and measures how long it takes to bounce back. Since radio waves travel at a known speed, the device can calculate the exact distance to the ground beneath the aircraft. This tells you your height above the terrain directly below — not above sea level, but above the actual ground. This is particularly useful during landing.

Modern GPS devices also include altimeters that calculate height using satellite signals, though these are generally less precise than barometric ones for aviation purposes.

Aviation is the most prominent field. Every aircraft cockpit has an altimeter, and pilots rely on it constantly. Air traffic control assigns aircraft to fly at specific altitudes to prevent mid-air collisions. Without an altimeter, maintaining safe separation between aircraft would be impossible.

Mountain climbing and hiking — mountaineers carry portable altimeters (often built into wristwatches) to track their progress, navigate terrain, and forecast weather changes. Because falling air pressure often signals incoming bad weather, an altimeter can double as a rough weather predictor.

Skydiving and parachuting — a jumper uses an altimeter to know when they've fallen to the altitude at which they must deploy their parachute (typically around 1,000–1,500 meters above the ground). Getting this wrong can be fatal, making the altimeter a life-critical instrument.

Military operations — soldiers, paratroopers, and military pilots all rely on altimeters for navigation, tactical planning, and safe operations.

Spacecraft and satellites — altimeters on satellites are used to map the Earth's surface, measure ocean levels, track glaciers, and monitor sea level rise over time. These are extremely precise instruments.

Meteorology — weather balloons carry altimeters to record atmospheric data at different heights, helping scientists understand how pressure, temperature, and humidity change with altitude.

Surveying and mapping — geographers and engineers use altimeters to measure the elevation of land, which feeds into the creation of topographic maps.

One important nuance — an altimeter reading always depends on its reference point, and there are two main ones:

  • Altitude above sea level (ASL): How high you are compared to the ocean's surface. A mountain's height is always given this way. If a mountain is "3,000 metres high," that means 3,000 metres above sea level.
  • Height above ground level (AGL): How high you are above the terrain directly beneath you. A helicopter hovering 50 metres above a hilltop that is itself 1,000 metres above sea level is at 50 metres AGL, but 1,050 metres ASL.

Pilots must keep both in mind. A barometric altimeter tells them their altitude above sea level; a radar altimeter tells them their height above whatever terrain is below. During a landing approach, the radar altimeter is what matters most — it tells the pilot how close the wheels are to the actual runway.

An altimeter is a measuring instrument for height above a reference level. It is indispensable in aviation, mountaineering, skydiving, surveying, and space exploration — anywhere that knowing your precise height is critical to safety, navigation, or scientific understanding. Its most common form uses air pressure to determine altitude, based on the reliable principle that air gets thinner (and pressure drops) the higher you go.
